questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,17),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b-{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,17)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-5≡b-5\,(\text{mod}\,17)
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x+5≡11\,(\text{mod}\,15)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $5$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+5-5 & ≡11-5\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,7),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a+{{field-1}}≡b+{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,7)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can add the same integer to both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+1≡b+1\,(\text{mod}\,7)
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,11),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b-{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,11)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-6≡b-6\,(\text{mod}\,11)
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Which of the following is congruent to $0$ modulo $15?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that 

$$
a≡0\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,a=kn,
$$

where $k\in Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $15$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $15.$

Therefore, since $15\,|\,60,$ we obtain

$$
60≡4\cdot 15≡4\cdot 0≡0\,(\text{mod}\,15).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $15.$

Therefore, since $4\,|\,52,$ we obtain

$$

$$

None of the other options are multiples of $4.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $13$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-26=(-2)\cdot 13.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-26≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13)
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,15),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b\,(\text{mod}\,15)
$$
questions.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $15$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-45=(-3)\cdot 15.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-45≡b\,(\text{mod}\,15)
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x≡26\,(\text{mod}\,12)?$
questions.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $12\cdot (-2)≡0\,(\text{mod}\,12)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡26+0\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ x & ≡26+0\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡26+12\cdot (-2)\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡26-24\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem:
A parodic holiday, International Talk Like a Pirate Day, was celebrated for the first time on September 19th, 1995. Given that January 1st, 1995, was a Sunday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week this holiday was celebrated for the first time.

*Hint: The year 1995 was not a leap year since it is not divisible by $4.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1995, and September 1st, 1995. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July,  and  August).

- There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April and  June).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and September 19th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to September 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(2)+28(1)}}+18.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,18≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+2(30)+1(28)+18 \\  & ≡5(3)+2(2)+1(0)+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $2$ days after January 1st, 1995, namely Tuesday.

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
Jacopo Peri's Euridice, modern opera's earliest known, fully surviving work, was first performed in Florence on October 6th, 1600. Given that January 1st, 1600, was a Saturday, use congruences to determine the day of the week on which the opera was first performed.

*Hint: The year 1600 was a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and divisible by $400.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1600, and October 1st, 1600. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, and August).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and October 6th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to October 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(3)+29(1)}}+5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,5≡5,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+3(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡5(3)+3(2)+(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+6+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡13\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date 6 days after January 1st, 1600, namely Friday.

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem:
Christmas in 2100 will be celebrated, as usual, on December 25th. Given that January 1st, 2100, is a Friday, use congruences to determine the day of the week on which Christmas will be celebrated in 2100.

*Hint: The year 2100 is not a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and is not divisible by $400.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 2100, and December 1st, 2100. 

- There are $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There are $4$ months with $30$ days (April, June, September, and November).

- There is $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and December 25th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to December 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(4)+28(1)}}+24.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,24≡3\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+4(30)+1(28)+24 \\  & ≡6(3)+4(2)+(0)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+8+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+1+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $1$ day after January 1st, 2100, namely Saturday.

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem:
You're given that January 1st, 2000, was a Saturday. Use congruences to determine the day of the week on November 4th, 2000.

*Hint: The year 2000 was a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and divisible by $400.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 2000, and November 1st, 2000. 

- There were $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 4th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to November 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(3)+29(1)}}+3.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+3(30)+1(29)+3 \\  & ≡6(3)+3(2)+(1)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+6+1+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡14\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡0\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as January 1st, 2000, namely Saturday.

questions.problem:
On November 16th, 1700, Spain's King Charles II died. Given that January 1st, 1700, was a Friday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week Charles II died.

*Hint: The year 1700 was not a leap year since it's an end-of-century year (multiple of $100$) and is not divisible by $400.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1700, and November 1st, 1700. 

- There were $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There were $3$ months with $30$ days (April, June, and September).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and November 16th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to November 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(3)+28(1)}}+15.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,15≡1\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+3(30)+1(28)+15 \\  & ≡6(3)+3(2)+(0)+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+6+0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+6+0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties
canonical_examples.problem: If $x + 8 \equiv 11\: (\textrm{mod}\,15),$ find an equivalent statement where $x$ is isolated.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that 

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a\equiv b \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a-c\equiv b-c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $8$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+8 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+8-8 & ≡11-8\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Integers That Are Congruent to Zero Modulo N
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following numbers is congruent to $0$ modulo $18?$

I. $-45$

II. $42$

III. $-54$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, recall that  

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $18$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $18.$

So, since $18\,|\,(-54),$ we obtain

$$
-54 \equiv (-3) \cdot {\color{blue}18} \equiv (-3)\cdot 0\equiv 0 \quad (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}18}).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $18.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Integers That Are Congruent to Zero Modulo N

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Simplifying Congruences
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $x \equiv 23\: (\textrm{mod}\,6)?$ 

I. $x \equiv 2 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

II. $x \equiv 3 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$

III. $x \equiv 5 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}6} \cdot (-3) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}6})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡23+0\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ x & ≡23+0\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡23+6\cdot (-3)\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡23-18\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Date Problems
canonical_examples.problem:
The opening ceremony of the first modern Olympic Games was held on April 6th, 1896. Given that January 1st, 1896, was a Wednesday, use congruences to determine the day on which the Olympic Games opened.

*Hint: The year 1896 was a leap year since it's divisible by $4$ and is not an end-of-century year.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1896, and April 6th, 1896. 

- There were $2$ months with $31$ days (January and March).

- There were $0$ months with $30$ days.

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and April 6th is given by

$$
d 
= \overbrace{31(2) + 30(0) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to April 1st}} + 5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2(31)+0(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡2(3)+0(2)+1(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6+0+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $5$ days after January 1st, 1896, namely Monday.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that two integers $a$ and $b$ are *congruent modulo* $n$ if they have the same remainder when divided by $n.$

Moreover, $a$ and $b$ are congruent modulo $n$ if and only if $n$ divides $a-b.$

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a-b = kn,
$$

where $k\in\mathbb Z.$ 

A convenient property of congruences is that we can add and subtract on both sides, just as with regular equations. 

Consider, for instance, the following true statement:

$$
22\equiv 10 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,12)
$$

The **addition property** allows us to add an integer to both sides. For example, adding $2$ to both sides gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22+2 & ≡10+2\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 24 & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is also a true statement since $24$ and $12$ both have a remainder of zero when divided by $12.$

Similarly, the **subtraction property** allows us to subtract an integer from both sides. For example, subtracting $9$ from both sides of our original statement gives

$$
\begin{aligned}22-9 & ≡10-9\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ 13 & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

which is a true statement since $13$ and $1$ both have a remainder of $1$ when divided by $12.$

In general, the addition and subtraction properties state the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Integers Congruent to Zero
tutorials.problem:
According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn,
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting $b=0,$ we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

*Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n.$*

For example, the numbers $10,$ $-25,$ and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5},$ so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ -25 & =(-5)\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 75 & =15\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Simplifying Congruences Using Integers Congruent to Zero
tutorials.problem:
Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5.
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n}).$ 

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡102\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x+0 & ≡102+0\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & \text{ }≡102+5\cdot (-20)\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡102-100\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5).$

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5,$ and $0 \leq  2 < 5.$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n.
$$

tutorials.name: Proof of the Addition and Subtraction Properties
tutorials.problem:
In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)-(b+c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)≡(b+c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

The subtraction property is proved similarly:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)-(b-c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)≡(b-c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $5$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+5-5 & ≡11-5\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x+5≡11(mod15)?

a
x≡11(mod5)
b
x≡4(mod10)
c
x≡6(mod15)
d
x≡5(mod4)
e
x≡11(mod15)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The addition property of congruences states that

a≡b⟺a+c≡b+c(modn).

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

a≡b⟺a−c≡b−c(modn).

We use the subtraction property to subtract 5 from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

x+5≡11(mod15)x+5−5≡11−5(mod15)x≡6(mod15)

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can add the same integer to both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+1≡b+1\,(\text{mod}\,7)
$$

observed_steps.name: Integers Congruent to Zero
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

tutorial.name: Integers Congruent to Zero
tutorial.problem:
According to the definition of modular congruence, we have that

$$
a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = b+ kn,
$$

where $k \in \mathbb{Z}.$ Substituting $b=0,$ we obtain

$$
a \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid a  \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad a = kn
$$

This gives rise to the following important fact:

*Any integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $n.$*

For example, the numbers $10,$ $-25,$ and $75$ are all are all multiples of ${\color{blue}5},$ so they are all congruent to $0$ modulo ${\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ -25 & =(-5)\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5) \\ 75 & =15\cdot 5≡0 & \,(\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.name: Simplifying Congruences Using Integers Congruent to Zero
tutorial.problem:
Let's try to simplify the right-hand side of the following congruence:

$$
x \equiv 102 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)
$$

By "simplify," we mean that we wish to transform the number on the right-hand side to be the smallest possible positive integer. In other words, we want to write

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < 5.
$$

When we add $0$ to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing $0$ as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to $0\:(\textrm{mod}\:{\color{black}n}).$ 

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  ${\color{blue}5} \cdot (-20) \equiv 0 \: (\text{mod}\:{\color{blue}5})$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ≡102\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x+0 & ≡102+0\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & \text{ }≡102+5\cdot (-20)\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡102-100\, & (\text{mod}\,5) \\ x & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,5)\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $x \equiv 102\, (\textrm{mod}\,5)$ is equivalent to $x \equiv 2\, (\textrm{mod}\,5).$

Our answer is correct because $102$ and $2$ both have a remainder of $2$ when divided by $5,$ and $0 \leq  2 < 5.$

**Note:** By the division algorithm, there is exactly one value of $r$ that satisfies

$$
x \equiv r \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n)\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 0 \leq r < n.
$$

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 11
?
Given that a≡b(mod13), construct a statement that also must be true:
29
29
28
23
26
25
a−{(29)(S0)}≡b(mod13)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

This gives rise to the following facts:

a≡b⟺a≡b+kn(modn)a≡b⟺a+kn≡b(modn)

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus 13 to one side of the congruence. Notice that −26=(−2)⋅13. Therefore, we obtain the following:

a≡b⟺a−26≡b(mod13)

observed_steps.name: Question 12
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying Congruences
observed_steps.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $7\cdot 3≡0\,(\text{mod}\,7)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡5+0\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\ x & ≡5+0\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5+7\cdot 3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5+21\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡26\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡5(mod7)?

a
x≡22(mod7)
b
x≡28(mod7)
c
x≡24(mod7)
d
x≡25(mod7)
e
x≡26(mod7)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 7⋅3≡0(mod7) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡5+0(mod7)x≡5+0(mod7)≡5+7⋅3(mod7)≡5+21(mod7)≡26(mod7)

observed_steps.name: Question 13
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying Congruences
observed_steps.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $15$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-45=(-3)\cdot 15.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-45≡b\,(\text{mod}\,15)
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying Congruences
observed_steps.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $11\cdot (-3)≡0\,(\text{mod}\,11)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡35+0\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ x & ≡35+0\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡35+11\cdot (-3)\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡35-33\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x≡35\,(\text{mod}\,11)?$
question.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $11\cdot (-3)≡0\,(\text{mod}\,11)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡35(mod11)?

a
x≡9(mod11)
b
x≡2(mod11)
c
x≡3(mod11)
d
x≡5(mod11)
e
x≡7(mod11)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 11⋅(−3)≡0(mod11) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡35+0(mod11)x≡35+0(mod11)≡35+11⋅(−3)(mod11)≡35−33(mod11)≡2(mod11)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $12\cdot (-2)≡0\,(\text{mod}\,12)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡26+0\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ x & ≡26+0\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡26+12\cdot (-2)\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡26-24\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡26(mod12)?

a
x≡5(mod12)
b
x≡6(mod12)
c
x≡4(mod12)
d
x≡3(mod12)
e
x≡2(mod12)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 12⋅(−2)≡0(mod12) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡26+0(mod12)x≡26+0(mod12)≡26+12⋅(−2)(mod12)≡26−24(mod12)≡2(mod12)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1896, and April 6th, 1896. 

- There were $2$ months with $31$ days (January and March).

- There were $0$ months with $30$ days.

- There was $1$ month with $29$ days (February) since it was a leap year.

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and April 6th is given by

$$
d 
= \overbrace{31(2) + 30(0) + 29(1)}^{\textrm{days to April 1st}} + 5.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31 \equiv 3, \qquad 30\equiv 2, \qquad 29\equiv 1 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\, 7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =2(31)+0(30)+1(29)+5 \\  & ≡2(3)+0(2)+1(1)+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡6+0+1+5\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡12\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $5$ days after January 1st, 1896, namely Monday.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Date Problems
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1995, and September 1st, 1995. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July,  and  August).

- There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April and  June).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and September 19th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to September 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(2)+28(1)}}+18.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,18≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+2(30)+1(28)+18 \\  & ≡5(3)+2(2)+1(0)+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $2$ days after January 1st, 1995, namely Tuesday.

$$

tutorial.name: Proof of the Addition and Subtraction Properties
tutorial.problem:
In this lesson, we've been working with the so-called addition property of modular arithmetic.

$$
a\equiv b  \quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad a+c\equiv b+c \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n)
$$

It's straightforward to prove the addition property by writing $a\equiv b$ in terms of divisibility:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)-(b+c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a+c)≡(b+c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

The subtraction property is proved similarly:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\, & ⟺\,a-b=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)-(b-c)=kn \\  & ⟺\,(a-c)≡(b-c)\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,17),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b-{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,17)
$$
question.worked_solution:
The subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$

question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x+5≡11\,(\text{mod}\,15)?$
question.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

We use the subtraction property to subtract $5$ from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+5-5 & ≡11-5\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x+5≡11(mod15)?

a
x≡11(mod5)
b
x≡4(mod10)
c
x≡6(mod15)
d
x≡5(mod4)
e
x≡11(mod15)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The addition property of congruences states that

a≡b⟺a+c≡b+c(modn).

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

a≡b⟺a−c≡b−c(modn).

We use the subtraction property to subtract 5 from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

x+5≡11(mod15)x+5−5≡11−5(mod15)x≡6(mod15)

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x+5-5 & ≡11-5\, & (\text{mod}\,15) \\ x & ≡6\, & (\text{mod}\,15)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x+5≡11(mod15)?

a
x≡11(mod5)
b
x≡4(mod10)
c
x≡6(mod15)
d
x≡5(mod4)
e
x≡11(mod15)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The addition property of congruences states that

a≡b⟺a+c≡b+c(modn).

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

a≡b⟺a−c≡b−c(modn).

We use the subtraction property to subtract 5 from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

x+5≡11(mod15)x+5−5≡11−5(mod15)x≡6(mod15)
question.knowledge_point: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

solution.reasoning: Subtract 5 from both sides while retaining modulus 15: x≡11-5≡6 (mod 15). This proves option c mathematically; no captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x+5≡11(mod15)?

a
x≡11(mod5)
b
x≡4(mod10)
c
x≡6(mod15)
d
x≡5(mod4)
e
x≡11(mod15)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The addition property of congruences states that

a≡b⟺a+c≡b+c(modn).

Similarly, the subtraction property states that

a≡b⟺a−c≡b−c(modn).

We use the subtraction property to subtract 5 from both sides of the given congruence, as follows:

x+5≡11(mod15)x+5−5≡11−5(mod15)x≡6(mod15)
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,7),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a+{{field-1}}≡b+{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,7)
$$
question.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can add the same integer to both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+1≡b+1\,(\text{mod}\,7)
$$

Question 3
?
Given that a≡b(mod7), construct a statement that also must be true:
5
5
1
3
1
1
4
2
a+{(5)(S0)}≡b+{(1)(S1)}(mod7)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The addition property of congruences states that

a≡b⟺a+c≡b+c(modn).

Therefore, we can add the same integer to both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

a≡b⟺a+1≡b+1(mod7)
question.knowledge_point: Using the Addition and Subtraction Properties

solution.reasoning: Adding the same number to both sides preserves congruence. The only pair of supplied choices congruent modulo 7 is 1 and 1, so a+1≡b+1 (mod 7) must hold. This is mathematically certain; no Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

feedback.worked_solution:
The addition property of congruences states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+c≡b+c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a+1≡b+1\,(\text{mod}\,7)
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,9),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b-{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,9)
$$
question.worked_solution:
The subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-2≡b-2\,(\text{mod}\,9)
$$

a≡b⟺a−2≡b−2(mod9)

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,11),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b-{{field-2}}\,(\text{mod}\,11)
$$
question.worked_solution:
The subtraction property states that

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-c≡b-c\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

Therefore, we can subtract the same integer from both sides of a congruence, keeping the modulus unchanged:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-6≡b-6\,(\text{mod}\,11)
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Which of the following is congruent to $0$ modulo $15?$
question.worked_solution:
First, recall that 

$$
a≡0\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,a=kn,
$$

where $k\in Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $15$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $15.$

Therefore, since $15\,|\,60,$ we obtain

$$
60≡4\cdot 15≡4\cdot 0≡0\,(\text{mod}\,15).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $15.$

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying Integers That Are Congruent to Zero Modulo N
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, recall that 

$$
a≡0\,(\text{mod}\,n)\,⟺\,a=kn,
$$

where $k\in Z.$ In other words, when $a$ is divided by $n,$ there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of $4$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $4.$

Therefore, since $4\,|\,52,$ we obtain

$$
52≡13\cdot 4≡13\cdot 0≡0\,(\text{mod}\,4).
$$

None of the other options are multiples of $4.$

62
c

d
30
e

a≡0(modn)⟺a=kn,

Question 10
?

Which of the following is congruent to 0 modulo 14?

a
−84
b
44
c
−40
d
−96
e
22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, recall that

a≡0(modn)⟺a=kn,

where k∈Z. In other words, when a is divided by n, there is no remainder. This means that any integer multiple of 14 is congruent to 0 modulo 14.

Therefore, since 14|(−84), we obtain

−84≡(−6)⋅14≡(−6)⋅0≡0(mod14). None of the other options are multiples of 14.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13)
$$
question.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $13$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-26=(-2)\cdot 13.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-26≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13)
$$

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying Congruences
last_observation.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $13$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-26=(-2)\cdot 13.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-26≡b\,(\text{mod}\,13)
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x≡5\,(\text{mod}\,7)?$
question.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $7\cdot 3≡0\,(\text{mod}\,7)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡5+0\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\ x & ≡5+0\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5+7\cdot 3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡5+21\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡26\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡5(mod7)?

a
x≡22(mod7)
b
x≡28(mod7)
c
x≡24(mod7)
d
x≡25(mod7)
e
x≡26(mod7)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 7⋅3≡0(mod7) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡5+0(mod7)x≡5+0(mod7)≡5+7⋅3(mod7)≡5+21(mod7)≡26(mod7)

question.html:
Question 12
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡5(mod7)?

a
x≡22(mod7)
b
x≡28(mod7)
c
x≡24(mod7)
d
x≡25(mod7)
e
x≡26(mod7)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 7⋅3≡0(mod7) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡5+0(mod7)x≡5+0(mod7)≡5+7⋅3(mod7)≡5+21(mod7)≡26(mod7)
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying Congruences

solution.reasoning: Since 26-5=21=3×7, 26 and 5 are congruent modulo 7. Thus x≡26 (mod 7) is equivalent to x≡5 (mod 7), making option e uniquely correct mathematically. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
Given that $a≡b\,(\text{mod}\,15),$ construct a statement that also must be true:

$$
a-{{field-1}}≡b\,(\text{mod}\,15)
$$
question.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

This gives rise to the following facts:

$$
\begin{aligned}a≡b\,⟺\,a≡b+kn\,(\text{mod}\,n) \\ a≡b\,⟺\,a+kn≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus $15$ to one side of the congruence. Notice that 

$$
-45=(-3)\cdot 15.
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
a≡b\,⟺\,a-45≡b\,(\text{mod}\,15)
$$

Question 13
?
Given that a≡b(mod15), construct a statement that also must be true:
42
42
40
48
45
50
a−{(42)(S0)}≡b(mod15)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

This gives rise to the following facts:

a≡b⟺a≡b+kn(modn)a≡b⟺a+kn≡b(modn)

So, we can add a multiple of the modulus 15 to one side of the congruence. Notice that −45=(−3)⋅15. Therefore, we obtain the following:

a≡b⟺a−45≡b(mod15)
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying Congruences

question.name: Question 14
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x≡35\,(\text{mod}\,11)?$
question.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $11\cdot (-3)≡0\,(\text{mod}\,11)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡35+0\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\ x & ≡35+0\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡35+11\cdot (-3)\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡35-33\, & (\text{mod}\,11) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,11)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡35(mod11)?

a
x≡9(mod11)
b
x≡2(mod11)
c
x≡3(mod11)
d
x≡5(mod11)
e
x≡7(mod11)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 11⋅(−3)≡0(mod11) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡35+0(mod11)x≡35+0(mod11)≡35+11⋅(−3)(mod11)≡35−33(mod11)≡2(mod11)
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying Congruences

question.html:
Question 14
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡35(mod11)?

a
x≡9(mod11)
b
x≡2(mod11)
c
x≡3(mod11)
d
x≡5(mod11)
e
x≡7(mod11)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 11⋅(−3)≡0(mod11) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡35+0(mod11)x≡35+0(mod11)≡35+11⋅(−3)(mod11)≡35−33(mod11)≡2(mod11)
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying Congruences

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡26(mod12)?

a
x≡5(mod12)
b
x≡6(mod12)
c
x≡4(mod12)
d
x≡3(mod12)
e
x≡2(mod12)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 12⋅(−2)≡0(mod12) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡26+0(mod12)x≡26+0(mod12)≡26+12⋅(−2)(mod12)≡26−24(mod12)≡2(mod12)
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying Congruences

$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

Which of the following is equivalent to x≡26(mod12)?

a
x≡5(mod12)
b
x≡6(mod12)
c
x≡4(mod12)
d
x≡3(mod12)
e
x≡2(mod12)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo n, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of n. This works because every integer multiple of n is congruent to zero modulo n.

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that 12⋅(−2)≡0(mod12) to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows:

x+0≡26+0(mod12)x≡26+0(mod12)≡26+12⋅(−2)(mod12)≡26−24(mod12)≡2(mod12)
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying Congruences

solution.reasoning: Since 26=2×12+2, 26≡2 (mod 12). Thus option e is mathematically equivalent to the given congruence. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $x≡26\,(\text{mod}\,12)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
When we add zero to both sides of a congruence modulo $n$, we can form an equivalent congruence by writing zero as an integer multiple of $n.$ This works because every integer multiple of $n$ is congruent to zero modulo $n.$

In our case, we add zero to both sides of the congruence and then use the fact that  $12\cdot (-2)≡0\,(\text{mod}\,12)$ to rewrite the right-hand side, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x+0 & ≡26+0\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\ x & ≡26+0\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡26+12\cdot (-2)\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡26-24\, & (\text{mod}\,12) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,12)\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
A parodic holiday, International Talk Like a Pirate Day, was celebrated for the first time on September 19th, 1995. Given that January 1st, 1995, was a Sunday, use congruences to determine on which day of the week this holiday was celebrated for the first time.

*Hint: The year 1995 was not a leap year since it is not divisible by $4.$*
question.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem using modular arithmetic.

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 1995, and September 1st, 1995. 

- There were $5$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July,  and  August).

- There were $2$ months with $30$ days (April and  June).

- There was $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and September 19th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to September 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(5)+30(2)+28(1)}}+18.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,18≡4\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =5(31)+2(30)+1(28)+18 \\  & ≡5(3)+2(2)+1(0)+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡15+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1+4+0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $2$ days after January 1st, 1995, namely Tuesday.

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,29≡1,\,5≡5,\,(\text{mod}\,7).

question.worked_solution:

First, we note the number of complete months between January 1st, 2100, and December 1st, 2100. 

- There are $6$ months with $31$ days (January, March, May, July, August, and October).

- There are $4$ months with $30$ days (April, June, September, and November).

- There is $1$ month with $28$ days (February).

Therefore, the number of days $d$ between January 1st and December 25th is given by

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to December 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(4)+28(1)}}+24.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,24≡3\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+4(30)+1(28)+24 \\  & ≡6(3)+4(2)+(0)+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+8+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+1+0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡8\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $1$ day after January 1st, 2100, namely Saturday.

$$
d=\overset{\text{days to November 1st}}{\overset{⏞}{31(6)+30(3)+28(1)}}+15.
$$

Now, note that

$$
31≡3,\,30≡2,\,28≡0,\,15≡1\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$

Therefore, writing the number $d$ modulo $7,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =6(31)+3(30)+1(28)+15 \\  & ≡6(3)+3(2)+(0)+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡18+6+0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4+6+0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡11\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the day of the week is the same as the date $4$ days after January 1st, 1700, namely Tuesday.
